entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 26 Eze 26:1-21 . The Judgment on Tyre through Nebuchadnezzar (TWENTY-SIXTH THROUGH Twenty-eighth Chapters). Isaiah ( Is 23:1-18 ), on the other hand, at the close of judgments, holds out the prospect of blessing, when Tyre should turn to the Lord. 1. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11500"/><div sID="gen20811" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11500"/><hi type="bold">2. Tyre--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Josh.19.29">Jos 19:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.7">2Sa 24:7</reference>), literally, meaning "the rock-city," Zor; a name applying to the island Tyre, called New Tyre, rather than Old Tyre on the mainland. They were half a mile apart. "New Tyre," a century and a half before the fall of Jerusalem, had successfully resisted Shalmaneser of Assyria, for five years besieging it (Menander, from the Tyrian archives, quoted by Josephus, Antiquities, 9.14. 2). It was the stronger and more important of the two cities, and is the one chiefly, though not exclusively, here meant. Tyre was originally a colony of Zidon. Nebuchadnezzar's siege of it lasted thirteen years (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.18">Eze 29:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1-Isa.23.18">Is 23:1-18</reference>). Though no profane author mentions his having succeeded in the siege, Jerome states he read the fact in Assyrian histories.<div eID="gen20811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Aha!--</hi>exultation over a fallen rival (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.21">Psa 35:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.25">25</reference>).<div eID="gen20812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">she ... that was the gates--</hi>that is, the single gate composed of two folding doors. Hence the verb is singular. "Gates" were the place of resort for traffic and public business: so here it expresses a mart of commerce frequented by merchants. Tyre regards Jerusalem not as an open enemy, for her territory being the narrow, long strip of land north of Philistia, between Mount Lebanon and the sea, her interest was to cultivate friendly relations with the Jews, on whom she was dependent for corn (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.17">Eze 27:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.9">1Ki 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.12.20">Ac 12:20</reference>). But Jerusalem had intercepted some of the inland traffic which she wished to monopolize to herself; so, in her intensely selfish worldly-mindedness, she exulted heartlessly over the fall of Jerusalem as her own gain. Hence she incurred the wrath of God as pre-eminently the world's representative in its ambition, selfishness, and pride, in defiance of the will of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.9">Is 23:9</reference>).<div eID="gen20813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20814" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">she is turned unto me--</hi>that is, the mart of corn, wine, oil, balsam, &c., which she once was, is transferred to me. The caravans from Palmyra, Petra, and the East will no longer be intercepted by the market ("the gates") of Jerusalem, but will come to me. <div eID="gen20814" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11501"/><div sID="gen20815" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11501"/><hi type="bold">3-4. nations ... as the sea ... waves--</hi>In striking contrast to the boasting of Tyre, God threatens to bring against her Babylon's army levied from "many nations," even as the Mediterranean waves that dashed against her rock-founded city on all sides.<div eID="gen20815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scrape her dust ... make her ... top of ... rock--</hi>or, "a bare rock" [Grotius]. God had delegated to him the universal earth-empire which is His (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.47">Da 2:47</reference>). The Son of God alone has the right and title inherently, and shall assume it when the world kings shall have been fully proved as abusers of the trust (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.15">1Ti 6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.12-Rev.14.19">Re 17:12-14; 19</reference>:15, 16). Ezekiel's prophecy was not based on conjecture from the past, for Shalmaneser, with all the might of the Assyrian empire, had failed in his siege of Tyre. Yet Nebuchadnezzar was to succeed. Josephus tells us that Nebuchadnezzar began the siege in the seventh year of Ithobal's reign, king of Tyre. <div eID="gen20820" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11508"/><div sID="gen20827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11508"/><hi type="bold">12. lay thy stones ... timber ... in ... midst of ... water--</hi>referring to the insular New Tyre (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.3">Eze 26:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.4">Eze 27:4</reference>, 25, 26). When its lofty buildings and towers fall, surrounded as it was with the sea which entered its double harbor and washed its ramparts, the "stones ... timbers ... and dust" appropriately are described as thrown down "in the midst of the water." Though Ezekiel attributes the capture of Tyre to Nebuchadnezzar (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.18">Eze 29:18</reference>), yet it does not follow that the final destruction of it described is attributed by him to the same monarch. The overthrow of Tyre by Nebuchadnezzar was the first link in the long chain of evil--the first deadly blow which prepared for, and was the earnest of, the final doom. The change in this verse from the individual conqueror "he," to the general "they," marks that what he did was not the whole, but only paved the way for others to complete the work begun by him. It was to be a progressive work until she was utterly destroyed. Thus the words here answer exactly to what Alexander did. With the "stones, timber," and rubbish of Old Tyre, he built a causeway in seven months to New Tyre on the island and so took it [Curtius, 4, 2], 322 B.C. <div eID="gen20827" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11510"/><div sID="gen20829" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11510"/>14. He concludes in nearly the same words as he began (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.4">Eze 26:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen20829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20830" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">built no more--</hi>fulfilled as to the mainland Tyre, under Nebuchadnezzar. The insular Tyre recovered partly, after seventy years (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.17">Is 23:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">18</reference>), but again suffered under Alexander, then under Antigonus, then under the Saracens at the beginning of the fourteenth century. Now its harbors are choked with sand, precluding all hope of future restoration, "not one entire house is left, and only a few fishermen take shelter in the vaults" [Maundrell]. So accurately has God's word come to pass. <div eID="gen20830" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11511"/><div sID="gen20831" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11511"/>15-21. The impression which the overthrow of Tyre produced on other maritime nations and upon her own colonies, for example, Utica, Carthage, and Tartessus or Tarshish in Spain.<div eID="gen20831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20832" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">isles--</hi>maritime lands. Even mighty Carthage used to send a yearly offering to the temple of Hercules at Tyre: and the mother city gave high priests to her colonies. Hence the consternation at her fall felt in the widely scattered dependencies with which she was so closely connected by the ties of religion, as well as commercial intercourse.<div eID="gen20832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20833" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shake--</hi>metaphorically: "be agitated" (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.21">Jr 49:21</reference>). <div eID="gen20833" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 15-21. The impression which the overthrow of Tyre produced on other maritime nations and upon her own colonies, for example, Utica, Carthage, and Tartessus or Tarshish in Spain. isles-- maritime lands. Even mighty Carthage used to send a yearly offering to the temple of Hercules at Tyre: and the mother city gave high priests to her colonies. Hence the consternation at her fall felt in the widely scattered dependencies with which she was so closely connected by the ties of religion, as well as commercial intercourse. shake-- metaphorically: "be agitated" ( Jr 49:21 ).
